title: That you may know (1 John 5)
hook: the letter ends: little children, keep yourselves from idols

segments.voice: Yesterday, we love because, and your line was he first loved us. Did you let yourself receive some love before you gave any? Day six hundred ninety-two.

Some letters bury the point in the middle. This one saves it for the end. First John is a long, circling letter: light and darkness, love and fear, little children, test the spirits. Then, in the last chapter, the writer gives what some readers take as his reason for writing all of it. And he signs off with a line that seems to come out of nowhere. Not grace be with you. Not peace. Just this: little children, keep yourselves from idols. No explanation, and then amen. Today, the last chapter of First John: the reason for the whole letter, and its strange parting shot.

The chapter opens with how love works in practice. In the King James Bible: "For this is the love of God, that we keep his commandments: and his commandments are not grievous." Not grievous: not heavy, not a crushing load. And then: "this is the victory that overcometh the world, even our faith." Then comes the purpose of the whole letter, in verse thirteen: "These things have I written unto you that believe on the name of the Son of God; that ye may know that ye have eternal life." That ye may know. Not hope, not guess, not lie awake wondering at night. Some readers hear the Greek verb here as settled knowing, the kind you don't have to keep checking. The letter has spent page after page on tests: do you walk in the light, do you love your brother. You might think the point was to make readers anxious. The writer says the opposite. He wrote so they could stop wondering and rest. One small note for anyone comparing Bibles. In the King James Bible, verse seven has a line about three that bear record in heaven: the Father, the Word and the Holy Ghost. Some modern translations leave that line out or put it in a footnote, and their notes explain why. Churches that teach the Trinity draw it from many passages and the early creeds, not from this one verse. And then the ending: "Little children, keep yourselves from idols." Scholars aren't sure what he had in mind. Maybe the temple statues in a city like Ephesus, where tradition places the elder. Maybe the false pictures of God the letter has been warning about. Maybe anything that quietly takes God's place. The letter doesn't say. It just leaves the line ringing, like a parent calling after you at the door: take care of yourselves.
screen: `WRITTEN SO YOU CAN KNOW, NOT GUESS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: name one idol, gently. Settle, and breathe. In the old sense, an idol is something carved and bowed to. In the wider sense some Christian teachers use, it's anything sitting in the center where something truer belongs. Your phone, maybe. Someone's approval. Money, a grudge, a plan for how life has to go. Let one come to mind. Don't scold it. Just name it, quietly, the way you'd name a houseguest who has stayed too long. Then let each breath move it one inch from the center. If you pray, you can rest on the old line from Psalm 46: be still, and know that I am God. The bell holds the time.
Idols. The strange parting shot that ends First John: keep yourselves from idols, after a letter written so its readers could know, not guess, that they have life.
Your line: keep yourselves from idols. Today, when a doubt or a worry shows up, notice it, and then go back to one thing you already know is true. Day six hundred ninety-two.

howItsDone: Some Christians read 1 John 5:13 as a word of assurance, and in teaching and preaching the letter's last line about idols is sometimes applied to anything, not only statues, that takes God's place in a life.

fork.setup: you're the elder, finishing a long letter to people you love. what's your last line?
options: warm greetings from the whole church.

fork.reveal: no greetings, no summary: "little children, keep yourselves from idols." he leaves it unexplained.

original.note: Greek: that you may know, from oida, to know. it's the verb in 1 John 5:13.

trapdoor: what you thought: a letter full of tests to pass.
what it means: the writer says why he wrote: so his readers could know, not guess, that they have life.
what a scholar hears: eidete, heard by some as settled knowing; and verse 7, where the King James and some modern Bibles part ways.

notes: 1 John 5:7 (the Johannine Comma) described as absent from the early Greek manuscripts and entering through the Latin tradition; confirm the phrasing is fair to Christians who hold the KJV text.
Tradition links the elder and the Johannine letters to Ephesus; framed as 'where tradition places the elder'. Confirm.
εἰδῆτε (perfect subjunctive of οἶδα) in 1 John 5:13; confirm form and pronunciation.
Readings of 'idols' (literal temple images, false teaching, anything in God's place) given without ranking.

Softened in review: 5:13 framed as what many readers take as the letter's purpose (the letter also gives purpose lines at 1:4 and 2:1); 'settled knowing' for oida framed as a common reading, since the oida/ginosko distinction is debated.

Editor review (2026-10-01): under the claims rule, the Johannine Comma passage no longer makes a manuscript or 'most translations' claim (cut 'isn't in the early Greek manuscripts... came in through the Latin tradition'); it now says only that the KJV has the line and some modern translations omit or footnote it (teach, screen, myth, trapdoor). A Keeper may restore the manuscript history with a cited source. Also 'many readers' to 'some readers' (twice), 'five chapters' cut, 'many Christians' in practice and howItsDone softened.
